newsitem.title: USA: Summers calls for stronger emerging bank systems.
newsitem.headline: Summers calls for stronger emerging bank systems.

text.p: Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers called Friday for bolstering banking and financial systems in emerging economies, saying that international capital markets depend on their strength.

"We have an obvious interest in minimizing the potential for weak financial regimes to trigger financial collapse, since the official community is often drawn in to absorb some of the cost," Summers said in remarks prepared for delivery at the Inter-American Development Bank.
He warned that global markets make it more likely that financial disruptions in one nation will spill across borders.

In the aftermath of the 1994 Mexican financial crisis, the Group of Seven industrialised nations called for averting future crises through such measures as tougher disclosure standards and beefed up surveillance by the IMF.

Earlier this year at a G-7 Summit in France, leaders put forth "key elements of what we believe should be the next phase of the agenda," Summers said. The G-7 plan centered on devising a global push to shore up emerging market systems.
"It is essential that the (IMF) take a more active role in helping to address the financial system vulnerabilities that can contribute to macroeconomic instability," Summers said.

Summers stressed that the international financial community "has a considerable stake" in domestic financial systems, saying that their strength helps to spread prosperity across borders through economic development.

He called for strict entry and reporting requirements, lending limits and other standards. And he warned that those rules must be enforced by a bank examination system, backed up by an independent authority with the ability to enforce compliance.
"Adopting a banking regime that looks good on paper won't head off the next crisis," he said.
The World Bank and regional development banks also have a role, Summers said, in assisting with the development of financial institutions that can keep up with the rapid growth of global markets.
He said the entire process would take years, predicting that it is "not one that will be competed a year or even a decade from now."

"As we have learned painfully from experience, making financial systems and the international financial systems less prone to major crisis is probably the dominant financial challenge of our time," he said.
